sysd-found-098.title: Website performance metrics: nine ways to judge a page
sysd-found-098.text: A web page can feel slow for nine different reasons, and each has its own metric. Website performance is judged by nine metrics. They are load time, time to first byte, request count, DOMContentLoaded, above-the-fold load time, first contentful paint, page size, round trip time and render-blocking resources. Load time is how long the browser takes to download and display the page, measured in milliseconds. Time to first byte is how long the browser waits for the first byte from the web server. It shows the server's general ability to handle traffic. Request count is the number of requests the browser must make to load the page fully, and the lower it is, the faster the site feels. DOMContentLoaded is the time for the full HTML to load, not counting CSS and other assets, and the sooner it happens, the sooner users see useful functionality. Above-the-fold content, the part of the page that fits in the browser window without scrolling, is seen first and often decides whether users keep reading. First contentful paint is when any content, text, image or background color, is first painted. Page size is the total file size of all content and assets, and the bigger the page, the longer it takes to load. Round trip time is a request going from the browser to the origin server plus the response coming back. Reducing it is a key way to improve a website's performance. Render-blocking resources stop other parts of the page from loading, so the more a page has, the greater the delay.

sysd-found-100.title: Data size units: decimal and binary prefixes
sysd-found-100.text: A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes, but the hardware often means 1,024. Data sizes are expressed as multiples of the bit and the byte, using either decimal or binary prefixes. Decimal prefixes such as kilo- are commonly used with bit and byte, but hardware sizes are usually binary. So each prefix 1000^n is customarily used for a close approximation of 1024^n. In decimal units each step up multiplies by 1,000, up to the petabyte, 1,000 terabytes. The IEC binary prefixes, such as kibi-, are accurate but not commonly used. A kibibyte is 1,024 bytes and a mebibyte is 1,024 kibibytes.

sysd-found-090.title: Network throughput: the speed actually achieved
sysd-found-090.text: A link rated at 100 Mbit/s that delivers 70 Mbit/s is running at 70% channel efficiency. Network throughput is the rate at which messages are successfully delivered over a communication channel. It is usually measured in bits per second, and sometimes in packets per second. Aggregate throughput is the sum of the data rates delivered over all channels in a network. Bandwidth is the maximum achievable speed or capacity, while throughput is the speed actually achieved, and it is always less than bandwidth. The physical medium, the processing power of system components and end-user behavior all limit it, and protocol overhead can make the useful rate much lower than the maximum. When a link with data rate R is shared by N active users, each can ideally achieve about R/N. Router and switch schedulers decide how the bandwidth is actually shared. Without fair queuing, users that send large packets get more bandwidth. Weighted fair queuing can prioritize some users when differentiated quality of service is provided.

sysd-found-092.title: Goodput: the throughput you can actually use
sysd-found-092.text: Not every bit that crosses a link is something the application wanted. Goodput is the amount of useful information delivered per second to the application layer protocol. It excludes dropped packets, retransmissions and protocol overhead, so it is lower than the maximum throughput. Maximum throughput is often an unreliable measure of effective bandwidth, because the achieved throughput is usually lower and protocol overhead eats into it. In file transmission, goodput is the file size in bits divided by the file transmission time.

sysd-found-091.title: Maximum throughput measures: four upper limits
sysd-found-091.text: A system's maximum throughput can mean four different things. The measures are maximum theoretical, asymptotic, peak measured and maximum sustained throughput. The highest data rate a system can deliver is used most often to compare systems, so comparisons must use the same definitions. Maximum theoretical throughput is the most data that could be sent under ideal circumstances. Peak measured throughput is measured on a real or simulated system over a short period, which suits burst transmission. Maximum sustained throughput is averaged over a long time and is likely the most accurate indicator for networks under constant load.

sysd-found-093.title: Latency vs throughput: two different questions
sysd-found-093.text: A passenger's trip on the London to New York air link takes the same time whether 100 or 10,000 passengers a day make it. That is the difference between latency and throughput. Latency is how long one operation takes, while throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time, and one does not determine the other. Throughput is counted in messages per second, the reciprocal of the unit for propagation delay, seconds per message. The two still interact. In reliable two-way communication, latency limits total throughput, as the bandwidth-delay product describes. When that product is larger than the TCP window, the sender must wait for acknowledgements before sending more packets, so flow control lowers throughput, as covered in {{ref:sysd-found-009}}. A cache can benefit latency, throughput or both. Beyond partitions, distributed systems also face a trade-off between latency and consistency, as the theorem covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-101}} states.

sysd-found-096.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation: sizing a system roughly
sysd-found-096.text: A billion requests a month sounds enormous, yet it works out to 400 requests per second. Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a rough calculation built on simplified assumptions that sizes a system's users, traffic and storage before it is designed. It is more than a guess but less than an accurate calculation or proof. Physicist Enrico Fermi emphasized approximating complex problems within an order of magnitude using simple calculations, and such sample calculations are called Fermi questions. For a design, ask about the desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed. A handy conversion guide says a month has about 2.5 million seconds, so 1 request per second is 2.5 million requests per month. Storage per record comes from adding up its fields. A paste has 1 KB of content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration length, a 5-byte creation time and a 255-byte path, which make about 1.27 KB. The primer advises clarifying with the interviewer whether to run these calculations at all.

sysd-found-193.title: Little's law: how many are inside a system
sysd-found-193.text: A store that sees 10 arrivals an hour, with an average stay of 0.5 hour, holds 5 customers on average. Little's law says the long-term average number of customers in a stable system equals the average arrival rate times the average time a customer spends there. It holds whatever the arrival process, the service distribution or the service order. It applies to any system and to systems within systems: in a bank branch it holds for the customer line, for each teller and for the whole branch. If the mean number in the system and the mean throughput are known, mean response time is their ratio. An average of ten jobs in the system at 50 per second gives 0.2 seconds. A system is stable when arrivals match exits. If arrivals exceed exits, the waiting grows without bound, and a system with limited space rejects the overflow, so its effective arrival rate is below the arrival rate.

openers.latency-throughput-and-back-of-the-envel: Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response. Its companions are bandwidth, the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path, and throughput, the rate at which messages are successfully delivered. Rough latencies of common operations, from cache reads taking nanoseconds to a transatlantic packet taking 100 ms, let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow. Tail latency is measured at a high percentile, such as the 95th, 99th or 99.9th, rather than as an average. This chapter also gives you the units for sizing data and the nine metrics used to judge a website's performance.

reviews.latency-throughput-and-back-of-the-envel: Latency and throughput answer different questions: latency is how long one operation takes, throughput is how many complete per unit of time, and bandwidth is the ceiling that throughput never reaches. Network latency adds propagation, queuing and processing delays, which is why round-trip time and the rough latency numbers matter, and why tail latency at a high percentile shows what an average hides. Those numbers, together with the units for data sizes, feed back-of-the-envelope estimates, and Little's law links arrival rate, time in the system and the number inside. Every technique for reducing latency, from indexes to compression, is a trade-off, as every design is.
